name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,210

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly and messily, so the letters come out in a jumbled order

blocks.note: taken as written, seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone bristles with irritation because they feel terribly sore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bristle' looks like the verb of the surface, but its letters rearrange into BLISTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A blister is a raised, painful patch of skin, so it is a kind of sore.

indicators.note: to finish off something here is to remove its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a male pig or wild pig

explanation.surface: An instruction to kill a pig and then a snake, like a hunter's to-do list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finish off' reads as 'kill', but it means cutting the last letter: BOAR loses its R to leave BOA.
explanation.definitionFit: A boa is a large constricting snake, and snakes belong to the reptile class of animals.

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
a fern is a leafy green plant
the first letter of 'out'

explanation.surface: A report that a blaze in a factory has been put out at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' suggests a factory but is a growing plant here, and 'in' is simply the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An inferno is a huge, raging fire, so the noun is a stronger synonym for a blaze.

clue.text: Yonder tree seen briefly in which he hides

indicators.note: something said briefly is cut short, so the word loses its final letter
whatever hides goes inside a cover, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then cut short to TRE
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man points to a distant tree, glimpsed briefly, in which someone is hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' looks like the man in the scene, but it is two letters tucked inside the shortened tree, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Yonder is an old word pointing to a place at a distance, the same job the adverb does for a far location.

blocks.note: a ram is a male sheep
to pant is to gasp for breath

explanation.surface: A startled sheep gasps and rears up on its hind legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rearing up' is a heraldic sense: a lion rampant on a coat of arms stands on its hind legs.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry an animal shown standing on its hind legs with forepaws raised is described by this term, exactly that upright posture.

blocks.note: first meaning: a moral failing or bad habit
second meaning: the bench tool with jaws that holds work steady (spelt vise in American English)

explanation.walkthrough: The British spelling covers both the moral failing and the workshop clamp; American English spells the tool vise.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a character flaw and a clamping tool with screw-tightened jaws used by carpenters.

indicators.note: round the bend means crazy, and crazed letters come out in a disordered sequence

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tells a great conductor that he drives them crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round the bend' sounds like part of a car journey after 'drive', but it is British slang for mad and signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi was a celebrated Italian opera composer, and maestro is a title of respect for great musicians.

clue.text: Cleaner part of fish that’s about right for cook

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: a char, or charwoman, is a British word for a domestic cleaner
a gill is the breathing organ of a fish
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A cleaner preparing fish takes the right portion to cook it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of fish' tempts towards fillet, but the fish part is GILL, which goes about R; a char is a British cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: To chargrill food is to cook it over intense heat so it is scorched, so it is a specific method of cooking.

clue.text: Go on, have it for breakfast!

blocks.note: first meaning: to talk at length without saying much
second meaning: a crisp grid-patterned batter cake eaten in the morning

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on' sounds like encouragement to eat, but it means rambling on; the breakfast item is the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means rambling vaguely, and the noun is a gridded batter cake often served with syrup at breakfast.

indicators.note: to spread is to stretch across, so one piece is laid across another and surrounds it

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
the moral of a story is its message

explanation.surface: It is a dangerous moment to be passing a message around.
explanation.walkthrough: The message is the moral of a story, which spreads around T.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortal wound or blow is one that causes death, so the adjective is a synonym for fatal.

clue.text: Choir’s range is extraordinary — you can bet on it!

indicators.note: extraordinary means out of the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A singer boasts that the choir's vocal range is remarkable, certain enough to wager on.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a sure-thing boast; the definition is literal, since gambling on results is central to the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The sport is a classic gambling event, with bookmakers taking wagers on every race, so the phrase describes it fairly.

clue.text: Spell words in prose they misspelt

indicators.note: a misspelt word has its letters in the wrong places, so the fodder must be put into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, nine letters

explanation.surface: A complaint about writers who misspell words in their prose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell' looks like the writing sense to match 'misspelt', but it is a magic spell.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjuror says this exclamation at the moment a trick succeeds, so it is a set of magic words.

blocks.note: first meaning: the promise I have given, as in 'you have my promise'
second meaning: a dated exclamation of surprise

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves read as one person speaking, but each is a separate meaning of the same two-word phrase: a promise made, and a cry of astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a solemn promise one has given and an old-fashioned interjection expressing astonishment, like goodness.

blocks.note: first meaning: an old-fashioned word for knickers or underpants
second meaning: the sliding compartments that make up a bedroom chest

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chest' suggests the body, which pairs with underwear, but it is a piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun is a dated term for underpants and also the sliding boxes in a bedroom cabinet.

clue.text: Very sad US soldier in wagon, retreating

indicators.note: retreating means moving backwards, so the word is read from end to start
in places one thing inside another, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a cart is a wagon
GI is the standard term for an American soldier

explanation.surface: A miserable American soldier sits in a wagon pulling back from the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreating' reads as the soldier's retreat, but it turns only the wagon round; GI, short for Government Issue, is the usual term for a US soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tragic causes great sorrow, so the adjective is a stronger synonym for deeply unhappy.

indicators.note: cuckoo is slang for crazy, and crazy letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written, seven letters

explanation.surface: The cuckoo has flown away, and that is a cause for concern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuckoo' looks like the bird that has gone, but it is slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: To agonise is to fret intensely over something, so the verb is a stronger synonym of fret.

blocks.note: first meaning: the 1950s popular music style
second meaning, read literally: in Greek myth Sisyphus was condemned to push a boulder uphill forever

explanation.walkthrough: Sisyphus was punished by the gods to push a boulder up a hill, only for it to tumble back each time; the question mark flags the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a popular music genre and, taken word by word, a boulder plus endless tumbling motion.

indicators.note: to be put in something is to be placed inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a chef is a cook

explanation.surface: An instruction to place the first item into the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooker' suggests an oven, but here it is a person who cooks.
explanation.definitionFit: Chief means principal or most important, as in chief reason, so it can replace the adjective meaning foremost.

indicators.note: stuffed is slang for ruined or wrecked, so the letters are broken up and reordered

blocks.note: the answer to the clue at 5 down, the composer

explanation.surface: A bird is stuffed, like a dish or a taxidermy specimen.
explanation.walkthrough: Stuffed birds suggest a roast or a museum, but the word means ruined; the letters of the earlier answer rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A diver is a waterbird, called a loon in North America, that hunts fish by plunging underwater.

clue.text: Seek a part of a church

blocks.note: taken as written
the tall pointed tower rising from a church roof

explanation.surface: Someone looks for a section of a church building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seek' sounds like hunting for the church part, but it is the definition and the clue is a straight charade.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to strive towards a goal or ambition, which matches the verb meaning to try for something.

clue.text: Said leader of opposition decorated after victory

indicators.note: after means following on, so one piece is placed behind the other
a leader goes in front, so only the first letter of the word is taken

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for victory, as in V for Victory
the first letter of 'opposition'
a cake that is iced has been decorated with icing

explanation.surface: A report of what the Leader of the Opposition said after being honoured following an election win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader of opposition' suggests the parliamentary post, but only its first letter is used; 'decorated' is the cake sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To have voiced an opinion is to have expressed it out loud, so the past tense matches.

clue.text: Polish off the extra dessert, last of all

indicators.note: last of all asks for the final letter of every word, so only the ends are kept

blocks.note: the final letters of 'the', 'extra' and 'dessert'

explanation.surface: Someone finishes off the spare pudding at the very end of the meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition fits the scene so well that solvers look for a synonym, but the letters come from the word endings.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish off food is an idiom for consuming it completely, so the simple verb meaning consume fits.

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the word is flipped and read from end to start

blocks.note: to flow is to run, as water does

explanation.surface: A driver runs down a wild animal on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run over' looks like a single phrase about a road accident, but it splits into the word and the turning instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A wolf is a wild canine predator living in packs, a clear example of an untamed beast.

clue.text: 1 down, say, exhausted having crushed old monarch

indicators.note: to crush something is to squeeze it tightly inside, so one piece is held within the other

blocks.note: spent means tired out
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A boa, worn out after squeezing a former king to death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks the cross-reference as an example: a boa is one kind of snake. ER is Elizabeth Regina, Latin for Queen Elizabeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A boa is one type of snake, and serpent is the literary word for any snake, so the earlier answer is an example.
